items.title: Haymaker re-posts its Nov 12 energy Trading Alert: the pick 'still has legs'
items.idea: Haymaker reposted a Nov 12 Ringside Access Trading Alert on an energy name and says it is still working nearly a week later. They push back on being seen as perma-bulls by pointing to a record of selling into big oil and energy rallies. The ticker is paywalled. The email also links a Nov 9 Thoughtful Money interview with Lyn Alden.
items.angle: Their energy pick came out the same week WTI fell 4% to $81.50 on an inventory build (see Innes). A long call that holds up through a bad physical print is worth noting. Open it to get the ticker.
items.tweetA: Interesting timing. One energy desk reposts a long call the same day WTI drops 4% on a 3.4M bbl crude build. Either the name has its own catalyst or someone's early. I'd want to know which.
items.tweetB: The best oil traders I know aren't perma-bulls. They're perma-sellers of rallies. Inventories sit 3% below the 5-yr average while Hormuz tankers get hit, and the market is selling oil anyway. That's the setup a rally-seller waits to buy.

items.title: Copper −5.6% (lowest since April), tin −8.2%: the AI-metals trade unwinds even though physical supply is tight
items.idea: LME copper fell as much as 5.6% to its lowest since April, and tin fell 8.2%. The selling hit London, New York and Shanghai at once. Copper was already down more than 10% from its peak. Speculative longs, which had been at record levels, have been liquidated and some have flipped short, and CTAs are adding to the momentum. Physical inventories in London and Shanghai are still draining, with squeezes in nearby contracts, but speculators chose to exit rather than fight over the last tonne.
items.angle: When price falls while the physical curve is in backwardation, that's a positioning flush, not a change in fundamentals. Watch the spreads. If nearby contracts stay squeezed while outright prices fall, the snapback will be violent. $FCX $SCCO $TECK
items.tweetA: Copper down 5.6% while nearby LME spreads are squeezing is the market telling you two different things. Futures say the AI trade is over. The warehouse says there's no metal. One of them is wrong by Christmas. $FCX
items.tweetB: Tin −8.2% in one day is the tell nobody is talking about. Tin is the solder in every server board. If the speculative AI premium is coming out of the smallest metals first, the copper move is a catch-down, not a verdict.

items.title: Druckenmiller flips bearish on copper at TomorrowX Austin, after backing the copper-AI thesis
items.idea: Speaking at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Stan Druckenmiller, one of the most prominent backers of the copper-for-AI thesis, said he is now short. Bespoke separately links part of Wednesday's 5%+ drop to his comments. Innes reads it as investors starting to question whether hyperscaler capex will turn into the physical metal demand already priced in.
items.angle: When the most famous holder of a thesis publicly reverses, that usually marks a reflexive low or the start of a long unwind. Druckenmiller rarely talks his book early, so this is more likely late-stage.
items.tweetA: Druckenmiller going public with a copper short tells you he's mostly done building it. The question for everyone else isn't whether he's right. It's who is left to sell after the record specs and the CTAs are gone.
items.tweetB: Same week: hyperscaler capex at $230B a quarter (+118% y/y) and Druckenmiller shorting the AI metal. Both can be true only if the capex is going into chips and not wire. Look at the bill of materials before you look at the price.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Copper)
items.title: Mercuria's Snowdon: underlying copper demand looks 'closer to recessionary'
items.idea: Speaking at an industry conference in Shanghai, Mercuria's Nicholas Snowdon said underlying copper demand looks closer to recessionary conditions than to healthy growth. That cuts against the story of an unprecedented investment boom. Innes argues the tariff-driven shipments into the US drained inventory elsewhere, and that this tightness was mistaken for strong end demand.
items.angle: The physical traders, who see real offtake, are telling a different story from the equity tape. If the tightness was tariff logistics rather than consumption, it reverses once the Comex–LME arbitrage closes.
items.tweetA: A $345B AI revenue run rate and 2.3% of GDP in hyperscaler capex, while the world's biggest physical commodity houses call copper demand 'recessionary'. AI is a chip boom, not a construction boom. Price it that way.
items.tweetB: Physical traders see the invoices. Analysts see the decks. When Mercuria says end demand looks recessionary while sell-side models assume an AI copper supercycle, I side with the invoices.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Copper)
items.title: Tariff trade reversing: the Comex–LME premium is collapsing and a Shanghai squeeze is pulling US copper back to China
items.idea: Lower confidence in more US refined-copper tariffs is shrinking the Comex–LME premium that drew huge shipments into the US. Shanghai's spot squeeze has also made it economic to move some US-held copper back toward China, which could unwind the inventory distortion the tariff trade created.
items.angle: This is a physical arbitrage in reverse. The metal that was stockpiled in the US against a tariff becomes supply for the rest of the world, a bearish overhang for LME and SHFE once it ships.
items.tweetA: The US imported a mountain of copper to front-run a tariff that may never come. Now Shanghai pays more than New York and the boats turn around. Tariff premia unwind on a shipping schedule, not overnight.
items.tweetB: Watch the Comex–LME spread more than the copper price. It's the cleanest real-time read on whether Washington still means it on metals tariffs. Right now it says no.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Copper)
items.title: 75bp more Fed tightening priced. Commodity FX ($AUD, $ZAR) faces a double headwind
items.idea: Markets are pricing roughly 75bp more US tightening. With a firm dollar and higher financing costs weighing on industrial demand, falling metals prices hit commodity currencies twice: once through the dollar's rate advantage and again through terms of trade.
items.angle: AUD and ZAR are the cleanest FX expressions of a metals unwind plus a hawkish Fed. The equity market may not have priced the growth signal that commodity FX is sending.
items.tweetA: The Fed is hiking into a commodity crash. That's 75bp priced while copper, gold and oil all fall 3-5% in one session. The last time a central bank tightened into falling input prices, it was cleaning up the mess a year later.
items.tweetB: If you want a short that works on both a hawkish Fed and the end of the AI-metals trade, it's $AUD. Two headwinds, one trade.

items.title: Nvidia under interim CEO Kress: FY growth guide raised to 75%, cloud backlog $2.5T (from $2T in 3 months)
items.idea: In her first quarter as interim CEO, Colette Kress raised next year's growth outlook to 75% from 70%. The cloud backlog is now $2.5T, up from $2T three months ago, and Vera Rubin brought in about $20B in its first ramp quarter. TSMC leadership was in Nvidia's offices, 'fully engaged in helping us'. Returning cash is a 'super top priority', and Nvidia is being more disciplined on circular financing of neoclouds. Even so, the stock rallied more than 5% on the call and closed about 3% lower (Innes).
items.angle: +$500B of backlog in a quarter, a raised guide, and the stock still reversed. That's governance and key-person discount, not fundamentals. Watch whether the market prices in a Huang return as an option.
items.tweetA: Nvidia added $500B of cloud backlog in 90 days and raised guidance, and the stock closed red. When a company beats this hard and falls, the market isn't pricing earnings. It's pricing who sits in the CEO chair. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Buried in the call: more 'discipline' on circular financing for neoclouds. That's the quiet line. If Nvidia stops backstopping its own customers, the weakest GPU clouds lose their cheapest source of credit. $CRWV $NBIS

items.title: Nvidia board split: ~3 directors open to bringing Huang back. Haas and Murphy in the CEO search. SEC probe and December testimony
items.idea: Board chair Harvey Jones said a specific no to Jensen Huang returning, but Semafor reports about three directors are open to it. Heidrick & Struggles is running the search, with Arm's Rene Haas and Marvell's Matt Murphy considered. An SEC probe is ongoing, there's congressional testimony in December, and The Information reports Nvidia's sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang in 2022 as an export-control workaround.
items.angle: Governance overhang plus an export-control investigation lands just as Trump meets Xi in Shenzhen. Any Huang-return headline is a big upside gap risk for shorts.
items.tweetA: Nvidia's board publicly said no to Jensen while three directors privately say maybe. That's not a board, it's a proxy fight waiting for a date. $NVDA
items.tweetB: If Rene Haas leaves Arm for Nvidia, the more interesting stock is $ARM. Losing a CEO to your biggest licensee's rival ecosystem would change Arm's roadmap politics overnight.

items.title: Anthropic IPO book: ~$400B institutional and ~$100B retail non-binding demand. VCs increasing stakes. Altimeter asked for $5B
items.idea: WSJ and CNBC report about $400B of institutional and nearly $100B of retail non-binding demand, more than SpaceX saw. Bessemer, Menlo and Accel plan to increase their stakes at the IPO, and Altimeter asked for $5B. Ticker ANT on Nasdaq. Revenue run rate is $81B (up $10B in a month), with more than $900B of compute commitments and over 90 pages of risk factors. Fully diluted valuation is about $1.5–1.6T at a price above $80.
items.angle: VCs usually sell at IPO, so insiders buying more is a strong signal. But $900B+ of compute commitments against an $81B run rate is the leverage to underwrite.
items.tweetA: $900B of compute commitments against an $81B run rate is about 11 years of current revenue already spoken for. The IPO isn't a bet on the model. It's a bet that revenue keeps compounding faster than the commitment schedule.
items.tweetB: Most IPOs are where VCs get out. In this one Bessemer, Menlo and Accel are buying more. When insiders add at a $1.5T mark, the bear case has to explain what they're missing, not the other way round.

items.title: The week's outages (air traffic, banks, NSA, Microsoft, United) traced to rushed AI-driven patches, not attacks
items.idea: More than half a dozen outages this week hit air traffic, banks, the NSA, Microsoft and United. Rubio: 'We are not under systemic attack.' Bank CEOs and the NSA told Congress that AI-driven patches are behind the outages (Washington Sun). AI models are finding many flaws in legacy systems, and hurried fixes not yet tuned in production are causing the disruptions. Parekh links it to the earlier Mythos-class model concerns.
items.angle: This is a new kind of operational risk: AI finds vulnerabilities faster than organizations can safely patch them. It's bullish for observability, testing and change-management vendors, and for cybersecurity, which Innes notes outperformed Wednesday.
items.tweetA: The outages weren't an attack. They were the defense. AI found the bugs, and humans shipped the fixes too fast. The bottleneck in cybersecurity just moved from finding flaws to safely deploying patches. $DDOG $CRWD
items.tweetB: Nobody's pricing this: if every AI-found vulnerability creates pressure to patch now, change-failure rates go up everywhere. The companies that sell slow, boring, tested deployment just became critical infrastructure.

items.title: California DMV pulls Waymo from freeways indefinitely: 'imminent hazard to public safety'
items.idea: After a driverless Waymo tried to get around a CHP traffic break on I-280 and an officer had to swerve to block it (a video with 3.3M+ views), the California DMV called Waymo robotaxis an 'imminent hazard to public safety' on freeways and pulled them indefinitely. Waymo had already paused freeway rides in May over construction-zone handling. Its last round valued it at $110B.
items.angle: This is a regulatory setback in AV's most important market, and freeway service matters for airport routes. It also affects Tesla robotaxi timelines.
items.tweetA: A $110B robotaxi company just got called an 'imminent hazard' by its home-state regulator over one viral video. AV regulation is now set by social-media virality, not miles-per-incident stats. That's a risk no model captures. $GOOGL $TSLA
items.tweetB: Freeways are where robotaxis make money: airport runs, long fares, high utilization. Losing them indefinitely isn't a PR problem, it's a unit-economics problem.

items.title: Trump meets Xi in Shenzhen, with Putin there too, as Washington splits between China hawks and doves
items.idea: Parekh notes the US is divided, including within the Trump administration, on whether to be a China hawk or dove ahead of Trump's meeting with Xi in Shenzhen this week, with Putin also attending. McDonough adds that the administration has further restricted advanced chip exports, and Xi urged Asia-Pacific nations to resist protectionism.
items.angle: Watch for a chip-export headline out of Shenzhen. With Nvidia's China file under investigation, any easing or tightening moves $NVDA, $AMD and Chinese AI names sharply.
items.tweetA: Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen in the same week Nvidia faces an SEC probe over Chinese export workarounds. The summit agenda and the chip stock are now the same trade.
items.tweetB: A US president holding a summit in Shenzhen, China's hardware capital, isn't a neutral venue. Every image from that trip is a signal about whether chips are on the table.

items.title: Gold, platinum and silver all at 52-week lows on the same day: only 20 times since 1990
items.idea: Copper fell 5%+ (about 19% peak-to-trough since its September highs), gold fell 3.2%, platinum 4.3%, silver 4.6% and crude about 4%. Gold, platinum and silver were all on pace to close at 52-week lows together, which has happened only 20 other times since 1990, most recently in September 2022. Bespoke plots those dates on the S&P 500 and finds they haven't usually marked major equity turning points.
items.angle: September 2022 was close to the low for precious metals before a multi-year bull market. A simultaneous 52-week low across all three precious metals looks more like a capitulation signal than a top.
items.tweetA: Gold, silver and platinum at 52-week lows on the same day. Only 20 times since 1990. The last one was September 2022, and gold roughly doubled from there. I'm not saying it repeats. I'm saying that's what it looked like last time.
items.tweetB: Precious metals at joint 52-week lows while the dollar hits an 18-month high and the 10y sits at 5%. This isn't a gold story, it's a real-rates story. The metals move when the Fed blinks, not before.

charts.desc: Chart 2: S&P 500 with every prior simultaneous gold/platinum/silver 52-week low since 1990 marked. Chart 1: copper's ~19% peak-to-trough fall from September highs.

items.title: Dow: three straight 1%+ declines (−4.1% w/w). The 52nd such streak since 1952 and the first since April 2025
items.idea: The DJIA fell 1.41% Monday, 1.64% Tuesday and 1.11% Wednesday, down 4.1% from Friday's close. That's the 52nd streak of three or more straight 1% declines since 1952 and the first since April 2025. The median loss across these streaks is 5.3%, but forward returns have tended to be better than usual. Innes adds that UnitedHealth was the main drag while the Nasdaq closed higher.
items.angle: The Dow is price-weighted, so a big UNH drop distorts the signal. With the Nasdaq up and the Mag 7 outperforming, it's a rotation inside a price-weighted index, not broad liquidation.
items.tweetA: The Dow just had its first run of three 1% down days since April 2025. Remember what April 2025 turned into? Forward returns after these streaks beat the average. The panic signal is usually the buy signal.
items.tweetB: Dow −4.1% on the week while the Nasdaq closed green Wednesday. When the price-weighted index is falling and the cap-weighted one isn't, the story is UnitedHealth, not the economy. $UNH

items.title: UBS still targets gold $5,000/oz by end-2027. BofA sees silver back above $70–75 next year
items.idea: Even after the precious-metals rout, UBS still sees gold reaching $5,000/oz by the end of next year, and BofA forecasts silver back above $70/oz (mid-2027 target about $75). Sinn asks whether these forecasts are crazy or sound. Gold is now below $3,750 and silver is testing $44 (Innes), so both targets imply 33–70% upside. The full analysis is paywalled.
items.angle: The gap between sell-side targets and spot is now huge. Either the banks are about to cut targets (a capitulation catalyst) or this is the setup Tavi Costa calls a mid-cycle correction.
items.tweetA: Gold at $3,750, UBS target $5,000. Silver at $44, BofA target $75. Those are 33% and 70% upside calls from banks that won't revise until the price forces them. Watch for the target cuts. That's usually the bottom.
items.tweetB: If BofA's $75 silver call is right, silver miners, which just had record ETF outflows and are down 50%+ in six months, are the most mispriced asset on the board. If it's wrong, the banks capitulate next. Either way the volatility isn't done.

items.title: Q3 2026 hyperscaler capex: $230B in one quarter, +118% y/y, nearly all of 2024's spend. 2027 consensus above $1T
items.idea: Meta, Amazon, Oracle, Google and Microsoft spent $230B on capex in Q3 2026, 118% more than Q3 2025 and almost as much as they spent in all of 2024. Analysts expect well over $1T in 2027. Lee argues the bubble case is weaker than a year ago because AI revenue growth has outpaced investment growth.
items.angle: A $1T+ 2027 capex consensus is the demand floor for $NVDA, $AVGO, memory and power, regardless of who runs Nvidia. Watch for any 2027 guide-down.
items.tweetA: $230B of capex in one quarter, about $2.5B a day across five companies. The market spent the week arguing about Nvidia's CEO while its five biggest customers wrote checks at that pace.
items.tweetB: Capex up 118% y/y and copper down 19% from its high. If AI were a construction boom, these two lines couldn't diverge. They are diverging, so it's a silicon boom with a small physical footprint.

items.title: AI capex at 2.3% of US GDP: bigger than Manhattan, Apollo or the 2000 broadband peak. Only the post-Civil War railroad boom compares
items.idea: The five hyperscalers' capex was 1.28% of US GDP in Q2 2025 and 1.33% for full-year 2025. It reached 2.3% of GDP over the first nine months of 2026. Lee says there's no 20th-century precedent: it's far larger than Manhattan, Apollo or the broadband boom. Arguably only the post-Civil War railroad boom concentrated the economy this much. Epoch AI estimates more than 70% of global AI compute is in the US, and that share is growing.
items.angle: The railroad analogy cuts both ways. That boom built lasting infrastructure but also caused the Panic of 1873. Concentration at 2.3% of GDP makes the macro cycle hostage to five capex budgets.
items.tweetA: AI capex is 2.3% of US GDP. The only precedent is the 1870s railroad boom. That boom ended in the Panic of 1873 and a six-year depression. The railroads still got built, and the equity holders still got wiped.
items.tweetB: Here's the macro problem: at 2.3% of GDP, a 30% capex cut by five companies is a 0.7pt hit to GDP. The Fed is hiking 75bp into an economy where five CFOs control a recession lever.

charts.desc: Chart 2: hyperscaler capex as % of GDP vs Manhattan Project, Apollo, broadband 2000, railroads

items.title: Amazon, Google, Meta and Oracle now spend more on capex than they make from operations. A first for Google in 22 years public. $300B+ equity raised in 2026
items.idea: The 'they can pay for it from profits' argument is gone. Amazon, Google, Meta and Oracle all have capex above cash flow from operations, a first for Google in its 22 years as a public company. Google, Meta, Oracle and others have sold or priced more than $300B in equity in 2026 (The Information). Microsoft, still FCF-positive, offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, over a quarter of its workforce, which some read as freeing capital for chips.
items.angle: Self-funded capex has become externally financed capex. That moves the AI trade into the credit and equity-supply cycle, and with $94B+ for Anthropic and OpenAI next, equity supply is the new risk.
items.tweetA: Google's capex just exceeded its operating cash flow for the first time in 22 years as a public company. The 'cash-funded AI boom' line is officially dead. Every dollar from here is borrowed or diluted. $GOOGL $META $ORCL
items.tweetB: $300B of hyperscaler equity issuance in 2026, $94B for Anthropic this week, OpenAI in Q1. Equity supply is the variable nobody models in an AI bull case. Supply eventually caps price, in stocks as in copper.

items.title: Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, over 25% of its workforce, possibly to free capital for chips
items.idea: In late October Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its workforce. Some speculated it was to free capital for more chips, even though Microsoft still spends less on capex than it earns from operations.
items.angle: Labor-for-compute substitution at the largest scale yet. If chips are replacing headcount on the budget line, that's the AI labor story showing up in corporate P&Ls before it shows up in BLS data.
items.tweetA: Microsoft offered buyouts to a quarter of its workforce to buy more GPUs. That's the clearest labor-for-compute trade any company has made in public. Expect the rest of the S&P to copy it within two earnings cycles. $MSFT
items.tweetB: 60,000 buyouts at about $200K fully loaded is roughly $12B a year, or about 3-4 weeks of Microsoft's capex. The headcount cut doesn't fund the chips, it signals what management values.

items.title: VC is mostly AI: Anthropic raised $95B and OpenAI $122B through Q3, but OpenAI's latest round raised only $11B of a hoped-for $30B
items.idea: Real US startup deal value has grown dramatically for AI and stagnated for everything else. Anthropic and OpenAI raised $95B and $122B respectively through Q3 2026. But appetite may be weakening: OpenAI's most recent round raised only $11B against a $30B target, and non-AI companies complain it's increasingly hard to raise.
items.angle: OpenAI raising a third of its target right before Anthropic's IPO is the first real crack in private AI appetite. It matters for OpenAI's Q1 IPO pricing.
items.tweetA: OpenAI wanted $30B and got $11B. Anthropic's IPO is 6x oversubscribed. Capital isn't leaving AI. It's leaving the private markets for the liquid version, and that's a big shift in who sets AI valuations.
items.tweetB: Through Q3, Anthropic + OpenAI raised $217B, more than most years of total US VC. Every non-AI founder is competing with two companies for the same LP dollars. The non-AI startup drought is a 2027-28 innovation gap.

items.title: AI ecosystem revenue at a $345B run rate (4.2x y/y). Anthropic at $81B, up from $9B in January
items.idea: Exponential View puts AI ecosystem revenue at a $345B annualized run rate in October 2026, up 4.2x y/y. Anthropic hit $81B in October (WSJ), up from $9B at the start of the year, though Q3 growth slowed versus Q2, possibly from customers switching to OpenAI. Exponential View argues Anthropic needs only about 2% monthly growth through 2030 to cover its costs.
items.angle: If 2%/month covers costs and the company has been compounding many times faster, the IPO debate is about the slope of deceleration, not survival. Q3's slowdown is the number to watch.
items.tweetA: Anthropic needs about 2% a month to cover costs through 2030. It just did roughly 25% a month for nine months. Even at a tenth of that pace, the math works. The bear case has to be 'growth goes to zero', not 'growth slows'.
items.tweetB: $345B of AI revenue against $1T+ of 2027 capex. A 3:1 capex-to-revenue ratio is where telecom was in 1999. The difference is that this revenue is growing 4x a year, and telecom's wasn't.

items.title: Ramp data: Anthropic paid adoption plateaued at 45% since July, but cohort spend is 10x y/y and $100K+ customers up 8x
items.idea: In Ramp's sample of 85,000 businesses, Anthropic caught up with OpenAI in H1 2026 as Claude Code took off and now sits at 45% paid adoption, but it has barely grown since July, mirroring OpenAI's plateau since mid-2025. Anthropic's IPO filing shows customers who spent in Q3 2025 spent about 10x as much in Q3 2026, and customers spending $100K+ grew 8x from end-2025 to Sept 30, 2026.
items.angle: Breadth has saturated and depth is compounding, which is the classic enterprise land-and-expand pattern. The risk is Lee's point: keeping this pace may need several more Claude-Code-sized launches.
items.tweetA: 45% of Ramp's 85,000 companies already pay Anthropic, and that number stopped growing in July. But the same customers spend 10x more. Adoption is done. Intensity isn't. That's a usage-based model doing exactly what it's supposed to.
items.tweetB: Both OpenAI and Anthropic have now hit a paid-adoption ceiling around 45% of businesses. The next leg of AI revenue isn't new logos. It's agents burning more tokens per seat.

items.title: ChatGPT: 1.2B weekly users, only ~8.5% pay. Codex is 63.3% of enterprise tokens from 17.3% of users. Ads at $1B ARR
items.idea: OpenAI says 1.2B people use ChatGPT weekly, up about 50% y/y. Gemini and Meta AI each have about 1B. About 100M pay (8.5%). Codex accounted for 63.3% of enterprise tokens despite only 17.3% of enterprise users using it. For individuals it was 16.5% of tokens from 0.7% of users. ChatGPT ads reached $1B ARR by late August.
items.angle: Token demand is concentrated in agents, not chat. The compute bull case rests on coding and agent adoption, not consumer MAUs. That's why Claude Code drives Anthropic's cohort expansion.
items.tweetA: 0.7% of ChatGPT's individual users, the Codex users, burn 16.5% of all tokens. A Codex user uses about 24x the tokens of an average chatter. The AI compute story is a coding-agent story with a consumer app on top.
items.tweetB: 1.2B weekly users, 91.5% free, $1B ad ARR. That's under $1 per user per year in ads. Meta makes about $50. Either ChatGPT ads are the biggest untapped revenue pool in tech, or chat users are worth far less than search users.

items.title: US imports of large computers (GPU/TPU proxy) hit a $500B+ annualized pace, up from $200B a year ago
items.idea: Census trade data has no Nvidia GPU category, but 'automatic data processing machines' minus laptops captures most GPU and TPU imports. That's above $500B annualized, up from $200B a year ago. Computer parts and accessories (HS 8473.30, such as drives and PSUs) more than doubled. The most advanced chips are mostly assembled by TSMC in Taiwan. DC Chartbook separately notes global semiconductor trade now exceeds oil and gas trade.
items.angle: This is a real-time, non-company read on AI hardware demand, and a trade-balance and tariff exposure. A widening goods deficit from chip imports could become a political target.
items.tweetA: The US imports $500B a year of AI servers, up 2.5x in a year. Global chip trade is now bigger than oil and gas trade. The most important commodity in the world isn't in a barrel anymore. It's in a rack. $TSM
items.tweetB: $500B of server imports is a $300B swing in the goods deficit in one year. Some administration official will notice that number before the next tariff round. AI hardware is a huge, unhedged tariff target.

items.title: Democrats won both houses on an anti-data-center platform. AI regulation near the top of the agenda in January
items.idea: Earlier this month Democrats won both houses of Congress in an election where many candidates ran against data centers. When the new majorities take power in January, AI regulation is expected to be near the top of the agenda. McDonough adds that Van Hollen will prioritize AI safeguards if he becomes Senate Democratic leader, and Jeffries was nominated for speaker 251-11.
items.angle: Data-center siting, power-rate politics and AI safety rules become 2027 policy risks for the capex chain: utilities, IPPs and hyperscaler permits.
items.tweetA: Democrats just won Congress partly by running against data centers. In January, every hyperscaler's $1T capex plan meets a Congress that campaigned against the buildings it needs. Power-hungry AI is now partisan.
items.tweetB: The AI risk nobody priced into the Anthropic IPO: a new congressional majority that ran against data centers. 90 pages of risk factors, and the biggest one was decided at the ballot box two weeks ago.

items.title: Claude Artifacts grows into a full workspace: Docs, Slides, Sheets, Whiteboards, Data dashboards, Design systems
items.idea: Claude Artifacts has grown from a pop-up pane into a whole section of the app, 'something like an AI-powered Google Drive'. It now includes Docs, Slides, Sheets, Designs, Data dashboards and Whiteboards that stay editable after the chat. TWiAI's tester built a brand design system from a GitHub repo of assets, planned episodes on Whiteboard, tracked a Shorts calendar in Sheets, and edited copy directly in Docs.
items.angle: Anthropic is moving into Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 territory the week of its IPO. That changes the TAM story from API and coding to the office-suite seat. A threat to $GOOGL Workspace, $MSFT Office and Canva-type tools.
items.tweetA: Anthropic is listing at a $1.5T valuation the same week its app quietly became an office suite. Docs, Sheets, Slides, Whiteboard, dashboards. The market is pricing a model company. The product is turning into Workspace. $GOOGL $MSFT
items.tweetB: The real moat in productivity software was never the editor. It was where the file lives. Once Claude keeps the doc after the chat ends, it's competing for the default save location, and that's a much bigger fight than chatbots.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Asia Open)
items.title: Anthropic priced at $83 (above $70–78), raising $68B+, $94B+ with the private placement. 6x oversubscribed, bigger than SpaceX's $86.2B
items.idea: Anthropic reportedly priced at $83, above the marketed $70–78 range, and upsized to raise at least $68B. With the $26B private placement, that's over $94B, beating SpaceX's $86.2B including the overallotment. The book is reportedly 6x oversubscribed. Innes: 'that money has to come from somewhere', and the market isn't swimming in spare liquidity.
items.angle: The IPO is a liquidity event that drains other risk assets. Watch whether the buying spreads beyond ANT Thursday or whether existing tech stays offered. That decides the next leg.
items.tweetA: $94B raised in one IPO means $94B of something else had to be sold. Look at what fell this week: software, Nvidia, Bitcoin, gold, copper. That's the funding list.
items.tweetB: SpaceX's $86B IPO in June came with three straight days of net retail selling, the first since the pandemic. Anthropic is bigger. If the pattern holds, the best trade isn't ANT. It's whatever got dumped to pay for it, a week later.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Asia Open)
items.title: The 'Anthropic shuffle': before SpaceX, retail sold MU, QCOM, AVGO, AMD, SMCI, with three straight net-selling days (Vanda)
items.idea: Before SpaceX's June float, retail sold existing tech winners (Micron, Qualcomm, Broadcom, AMD, Super Micro) to raise cash. Vanda Research recorded three straight sessions of net single-stock selling, something not seen since the early pandemic. The pre-Anthropic pattern looks similar: software shares took the most punishment, and tokenized Anthropic exposure has tracked Nvidia lower.
items.angle: Mega-IPOs create a predictable funding-selloff window. That suggests a tactical buy of the names sold to fund allocations once the IPO trades.
items.tweetA: Every mega-IPO this year has had the same footprint: retail sells its winners to fund the new thing. SpaceX in June, Anthropic now. If you're watching $MU or $AVGO dip into an IPO date, that's not news. It's a funding calendar.
items.tweetB: Tokenized Anthropic exposure tracked Nvidia lower for weeks before the IPO. The crypto-wrapped pre-IPO market was a live read on how ANT would trade, and it said 'like a chip stock'.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Asia Open)
items.title: Goldman desk: volumes 20% below the 2-week average. HFs 6% better buyers with a 56% short ratio. Long-only 15% better sellers
items.idea: Goldman desk flows show trading activity 20% below the recent two-week average. Hedge funds were 6% better buyers but with a 56% short ratio. Long-only accounts were 15% better sellers, mostly in tech, materials and communication services. Credit saw modest widening with little new deterioration in hyperscaler or data-center credit. The S&P had a fifth straight decline and keeps failing at its 200-day moving average, while the Nasdaq closed higher and the Mag 7 outperformed the other 493.
items.angle: Long-only de-risking on low volume, while credit holds, points to rotation and IPO funding rather than a credit-led risk-off. That's the key difference from a real top.
items.tweetA: Long-only 15% better sellers on 20% lighter volume, and credit spreads barely moved. That's not a crash. It's real money raising cash for an IPO allocation. Stress shows up in credit first, and credit is calm.
items.tweetB: Hedge funds 'bought' with a 56% short ratio, so more than half their activity was shorting. The net-buyer headline hides a desk that's leaning short into the biggest IPO in history.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Asia Open)
items.title: October FOMC minutes: nearly all members expect more tightening. Waller keeps a 50bp December hike in play (10–15% priced)
items.idea: The October minutes showed nearly all policymakers anticipate further tightening, and Christopher Waller has kept a potential 50bp December move in the conversation. The market assigns only a 10–15% probability to 50bp. Even so, the 10-year rallied toward 5.05% on the oil drop and a solid 20-year auction, and the dollar hit fresh 18-month highs. TS Lombard (via DC Chartbook) says its dollar bull/bear indicator is the strongest since 2023.
items.angle: A hawkish Fed, a strong dollar and a commodities crash is a deflationary impulse the Fed is fighting with hikes. The risk is overtightening into a cooling industrial economy.
items.tweetA: A Fed governor floats 50bp in December, the market prices 10-15%, and the long end rallies anyway. Bonds are calling the policy mistake before the Fed makes it.
items.tweetB: Dollar at an 18-month high, 10y at 5%, and TS Lombard's dollar indicator at its strongest since 2023. Everyone spent 2025 calling the end of King Dollar. It just took the crown back.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Asia Open)
items.title: Oil 'trades the barrels, not the bombs': WTI −4% to $81.50 on a 3.38M bbl build despite US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island
items.idea: WTI fell 4% to $81.50 and Brent 2.5% to about $91 after US crude inventories rose 3.38M bbl against roughly 1M expected. Gasoline built by more than 5M bbl and distillates beat forecasts too. Total crude stocks are still about 3% below the five-year seasonal average. The headlines: US strikes on Qeshm Island, continuing tanker attacks around Hormuz, and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. Even so, smaller tankers keep Gulf shipments flowing, and October flows reportedly hit a wartime high.
items.angle: A $10 WTI–Brent gap and record wartime Gulf flows mean the risk premium has been arbitraged away by logistics. The asymmetry is that one successful Hormuz closure resets everything.
items.tweetA: US strikes on an Iranian island, Iran hits a US base in Kuwait, tankers attacked in Hormuz, and oil falls 4%. Gulf flows hit a wartime high in October. The market has decided small tankers beat big bombs. That holds until it doesn't. $XLE
items.tweetB: Brent $91, WTI $81.50. A $9-10 spread is the war premium living entirely in seaborne barrels. US inland crude is pricing the inventory build, and Brent is pricing Hormuz. If you want Gulf risk without the US glut, it's in the spread.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Asia Open)
items.title: Gold below $3,750, silver tests $44, Bitcoin hit: liquidity vs solvency, the first thing sold for cash
items.idea: Gold fell nearly 3% to below $3,750, silver tested $44, and Bitcoin took another beating. Some selling may be investors raising cash for Anthropic, especially in crypto, though the hawkish Fed does plenty of damage alone. Innes's framework: gold can be long-term insurance against financial instability and still be one of the first things sold when investors need cash. Central banks keep buying, but leveraged holders liquidate when losses elsewhere demand it.
items.angle: That's a liquidity sell, not a solvency verdict. If central-bank buying holds while leveraged longs clear, the sell-off sets up the next leg, as Costa argues.
items.tweetA: Gold isn't failing as a hedge. It's working as an ATM. When investors need cash for a $94B IPO allocation, they sell the thing that's liquid and still up on the year. That's not a top signal, it's a funding signal.
items.tweetB: Bitcoin, gold and copper all sold off on the same day for three different reasons: IPO cash-raising, real rates and the AI-metals unwind. When unrelated assets fall together, the common factor is liquidity, and liquidity comes back.

items.title: 'Does the customer still pay when AI can check the work?' Santos cut his accounting bill 80%+
items.idea: Santos cut his firm's accounting bill by more than 80%. The premium was never for quality. It existed because vetting a cheaper provider required an in-house bookkeeper or controller, so going cheap was the riskier career move ('nobody got fired for buying IBM'). AI lets customers check the work themselves, which removes the perceived risk of a low-cost vendor and with it the premium. The AI-forward firm they chose is faster and makes fewer errors than the non-AI firms they surveyed.
items.angle: This is the cleanest description yet of how AI deflates services pricing: not by replacing the provider but by removing the verification cost that protected incumbents' margins. Short fear-based trust, long earned trust.
items.tweetA: AI isn't killing accounting firms by doing the accounting. It's killing them by letting the client check it. The premium was always a tax on the cost of verification, and verification just became free.
items.tweetB: An 80% cut to a services bill isn't a productivity gain. It's a margin transfer from vendor to customer. Every 'AI roll-up' assuming it keeps the savings should run that number before buying the next firm.

items.title: AI roll-ups in accounting and legal: sponsors bake in cost savings, but customers claw them back. Harvey and Legora disrupt the firms they sell to
items.idea: Accounting roll-up multiples are rising, but most theses only bake in cost cuts. Santos's diligence found many customers pushing back on price. Tax prep is the most automated, bookkeeping is getting there, and advisory is the most defensible. In legal, Harvey and Legora are sold to law firms but undermine their model as clients demand savings back. The bigger threat is Claude and other tools clients use themselves to strip out clerical work. Santos moved legal from fixed fees to hourly, paying top partners only 'to opine, not to produce'.
items.angle: PE roll-ups of AI-disrupted services look like a classic sponsor trap. Avoid buying the vendor and own the customer that captures the savings.
items.tweetA: PE is paying higher multiples for accounting firms on an AI cost-savings thesis. The customers are already using AI to demand those savings back. You can't capitalize margin your client can see through.
items.tweetB: Legal is moving from fixed fees to hourly, the opposite of what everyone predicted. Clients do the clerical work with AI and pay the partner only to opine. The billable hour isn't dying. It's being cut down to the expensive part.

items.title: Investment framework: own services that AI makes more valuable, ones that price outcomes, not tokens, seats or hours
items.idea: Santos would 'rather own businesses that technology aids than technology businesses', because tech gets cheaper and easier to copy while the customer relationship doesn't. In old enterprise software, services were a sub-20% margin business against 80% for software. Now services matter more than ever. The winners: trust-heavy services that don't rely on friction or obfuscation, whose inputs customers can't easily distill, that price outcomes not inputs, and whose value rises with AI. Munger: 'Invert, always invert.'
items.angle: This inverts the SaaS-era services discount. If it's right, outcome-priced services trade up while seat-priced SaaS trades down, which fits the software selling seen this week.
items.tweetA: For 20 years VCs said services margins kill a company: 20% vs software's 80%. AI flips it. Software gets cheap to copy, and the trusted human relationship doesn't. The 2030s compounder might be a services firm.
items.tweetB: The test: does the customer value your service more or less once they have Claude? If less, you're selling friction. If more, you're selling judgment. Run your whole portfolio through that one question.

items.title: Silver miners: largest outflows on record from the sector's biggest ETF, down 50%+ in six months. 'Capitulation phase'
items.idea: Tavi Costa reports that silver miners just had their largest outflows on record from the sector's biggest ETF ($SIL), and the group is down more than 50% in six months. He calls it the capitulation phase and is revisiting the precious-metals thesis with a set of charts to judge whether this is a bear market or a mid-cycle correction. 'Never let a good crisis go to waste.'
items.angle: Record outflows, joint 52-week lows in gold, silver and platinum (Bespoke), and BofA still at $75 silver is a classic contrarian setup. The risk is that the Fed keeps hiking and real rates keep rising.
items.tweetA: Record outflows from silver miners, down 50%+ in six months, while BofA still targets $75 silver. Either the sell-side is about to capitulate or the ETF holders just sold the bottom. Flows usually break first. $SIL $SILJ
items.tweetB: Silver miners are leveraged silver, and silver is leveraged gold. A 50% drawdown in the miners on maybe a 30% drop in the metal is the leverage working in reverse. It works the other way too, and there's a lot less money left in it now.

items.title: Cantwell and Rounds ask White House AI chief Clayton for an immediate national AI-cyber plan, with no attacker identified
items.idea: Senators Maria Cantwell (D) and Mike Rounds (R) asked White House AI chief Jay Clayton to 'take immediate action' on a national strategy protecting infrastructure, financial institutions and software from AI-aided cyberattacks. Clayton told lawmakers the outages were technical and maintenance failures with 'no evidence of nefarious action', and officials said they weren't connected. No plan or rule has taken effect. Fulcrum: 'urgency needs no attacker.' Triggers to watch before January 2027 are a written White House strategy, a hearing, or statutory language.
items.angle: A bipartisan AI-cyber mandate, especially mandatory incident reporting for AI-assisted activity, would bring compliance spending to banks and infrastructure. Bullish for cyber vendors.
items.tweetA: Washington just learned AI's patch cadence can take down air traffic, banks and the NSA in one week without any attacker. A bipartisan bill will follow. When Congress gets scared without an enemy, it writes compliance mandates, and someone sells the compliance. $CRWD $PANW
items.tweetB: The outages were caused by AI-driven fixes, and Congress is responding with an 'AI attack' plan. If the rule targets attackers instead of change management, it'll miss the actual failure.

items.title: Iran hits a US-used airbase in Kuwait and targets in Bahrain after US strikes on Qeshm Island
items.idea: Iran attacked a US-used airbase in Kuwait and targets in Bahrain after the US bombed Iran's Qeshm Island (Al Jazeera). Separately, Defense Secretary Hegseth made a surprise visit to Venezuela and renewed military ties, less than a year after the US captured President Maduro.
items.angle: Direct Iranian strikes on Gulf Cooperation Council host states raise the risk to Gulf infrastructure, yet oil fell 4%. That gap between geopolitics and price is the trade.
items.tweetA: Iran just struck US positions in Kuwait and Bahrain, two GCC states, and Brent closed at $91, down on the day. The market is pricing Hormuz flows, not Iranian intent. One hit on a loading terminal flips that.
items.tweetB: Hegseth renewing military ties in Venezuela the same week Iran escalates in the Gulf. Washington is building a Western Hemisphere oil backstop in real time. Heavy crude from Venezuela is the hedge against a Gulf disruption.

items.title: A Senate committee rejects Jim O'Neill's NSF nomination after GOP chair Cassidy questions his defense of science
items.idea: A Senate committee rejected Jim O'Neill's nomination to lead the National Science Foundation after Republican chair Bill Cassidy questioned his defense of science (The Guardian). It's a rare intra-party rejection of a nominee to lead a federal science agency.
items.angle: NSF leadership uncertainty affects federal basic-research funding pipelines (AI, quantum, materials) and university labs.
items.tweetA: A Republican-chaired committee just rejected a Republican president's NSF pick over his commitment to science. When a party's own senators draw a line on research funding, the budget fight that follows is about more than one nominee.
items.tweetB: The US is spending 2.3% of GDP on private AI capex while the agency that funds basic research can't get a director confirmed. The public-research pipeline that seeds the next decade's breakthroughs is running on autopilot.

items.title: Nvidia speeds up pay raises as interim CEO Kress works on morale while Jensen Huang pursues a return
items.idea: The FT reports Nvidia is accelerating pay increases as interim CEO Colette Kress tries to improve staff morale, while founder Jensen Huang pursues a return.
items.angle: Accelerated raises at a company with a CEO vacuum are a retention defense. They signal fear of talent flight to competitors or neoclouds during the governance fight.
items.tweetA: Nvidia is speeding up raises to stop people leaving. When the most valuable chip company in the world pays to keep its engineers during a CEO fight, the talent market for AI hardware is tighter than any GPU.
items.tweetB: Retention raises, a split board, an SEC probe and a founder trying to return. Nvidia's opex line is about to carry a governance tax. Watch the gross-to-operating margin spread next quarter. $NVDA

items.title: Correlation Ventures: startups burning more than $400K a month are about 5x more likely to fail
items.idea: Data from Correlation Ventures suggests startups burning more than $400K a month are about five times as likely to go out of business as those below that line. The TWiST VC panel also says don't be too coachable: LAUNCH scores argumentativeness favorably, and Tim Draper wants founders to 'fight it in their head for a while'.
items.angle: In a market where AI megarounds hoover up capital (OpenAI and Anthropic took $217B), a hard $400K burn line is a practical survival rule for everyone else.
items.tweetA: $400K a month is the startup death line, with a 5x failure rate above it. Now compare that to AI startups raising $100M seed rounds to buy GPUs. Most of the 2026 AI cohort is above the line on day one.
items.tweetB: The most valuable founder trait, according to the people writing the checks, is ignoring the people writing the checks. Coachability is overrated when your VC's advice is shaped by their fund's timeline, not your company's.

items.title: Annual employee tender offers become standard as companies stay private longer. McClure wants the same for LPs
items.idea: Companies are staying private longer, so annual corporate tender offers for employee liquidity are becoming more common. Dave McClure argues investors need something similar. Tim Draper also built a fantasy-football app for investors just by prompting Grok, and warns vibecoded apps should stay minimal because added features eventually break things.
items.angle: Regular private liquidity is part of why SpaceX and Anthropic could wait until they were $1T+. The IPO is becoming the last exit, not the first.
items.tweetA: Annual tender offers mean employees don't need an IPO to get paid. That's why the companies going public now are $1.5T monsters, not $5B growth stories. Public investors only get the end of the compounding curve.
items.tweetB: VCs want LP liquidity programs while OpenAI raised $11B of a $30B target. Private markets are building their own exit plumbing because the IPO window only fits the biggest names.

items.title: TS Lombard/Blitz: no credit crisis. HY tech spreads wider but have been wider before, and consumer staples spreads have collapsed
items.idea: TS Lombard's Steven Blitz: 'Looking into the bond market to find a crisis in spreads, there is none to be found.' HY technology spreads have widened but have been wider before, while consumer staples spreads have collapsed. 'Nothing like a little inflation to boost expectations for the ability to service debt.' This fits Goldman's desk seeing little new deterioration in hyperscaler and data-center credit.
items.angle: The tech/staples spread split is the market saying pricing power beats growth capex. Staples issuers inflate their way into better coverage while AI-adjacent HY carries the capex risk.
items.tweetA: HY tech spreads widening while consumer staples spreads collapse. Credit markets have decided inflation helps a cereal company service debt and hurts a GPU cloud. That's the most 2026 sentence I've written.
items.tweetB: Everyone's hunting for the AI credit crack. TS Lombard looked and found nothing, while Google's capex now exceeds its cash flow. Either credit is complacent or the equity market is panicking about the wrong thing. I lean complacent.

items.title: TS Lombard dollar bull/bear indicator at its strongest since 2023 and rising, as US data surprises to the upside
items.idea: TS Lombard's Daniel von Ahlen: the dollar has gained more ground over the past month as US macro data keeps surprising to the upside, and their dollar bull/bear indicator is at its strongest since 2023 and rising. Innes separately notes DXY at fresh 18-month highs.
items.angle: A rising dollar plus a hawkish Fed is a headwind for EM, commodities and US multinational earnings in Q1 2027 guidance.
items.tweetA: TS Lombard's dollar indicator is at its strongest since 2023. The consensus 2026 trade was de-dollarization, and the market is doing the opposite. Gold at a 52-week low is the other side of the same chart.
items.tweetB: US data keeps beating, the dollar keeps rising, and the Fed keeps hiking. Strong economy, strong currency, tight policy: that combination usually breaks something outside the US first. Watch EM FX.

items.title: Russell 2000 death cross, the first in over a year. The R2K was higher 12 months later in 10 of 12 cases since 1987
items.idea: The Russell 2000's 50-day moving average crossed below its 200-day today for the first time in more than a year. In 10 of the 12 instances since 1987, the index was higher 12 months later. ICYMI from Daily Chartbook: more than half of Nasdaq-100 members are in a bear market, and the valuation premium of the largest US companies has narrowed.
items.angle: Death crosses are lagging signals with good forward returns. Combined with the Dow streak (Bespoke), the breadth washout is getting stretched.
items.tweetA: Russell 2000 death cross. 10 of 12 since 1987 were higher a year later. The scariest-sounding technical signal has an 83% hit rate as a buy signal. $IWM
items.tweetB: More than half the Nasdaq-100 is in a bear market while the index is near its highs, and the R2K just death-crossed. This isn't a broad sell-off. It's a market of about 10 stocks and 2,000 casualties.

items.title: BlackRock: CAPE vs forward P/E, 'choose your fighter'
items.idea: Daily Chartbook features a BlackRock chart comparing CAPE (cyclically adjusted P/E) with forward P/E for US equities, framed as 'choose your fighter': the two give very different valuation readings depending on whether you trust trailing normalized earnings or forward AI-era estimates.
items.angle: With hyperscaler earnings now externally financed, the gap between trailing and forward valuation is largely a bet on whether 2027 AI earnings arrive.
items.tweetA: CAPE says expensive. Forward P/E says fine. The gap between them is exactly one assumption: that 2027 AI earnings show up. That's not a valuation debate. It's a single-factor bet.
items.tweetB: Forward P/E uses analysts' earnings. CAPE uses earnings that actually happened. In a year when Google's capex exceeded its cash flow, I'd weight the one that can't be revised.

items.title: Consensus is not expecting much from the S&P 500 in 2027 (Authers/Bloomberg)
items.idea: A John Authers (Bloomberg) chart shows the 2027 S&P 500 outlook consensus is unusually muted. The Authers column is titled 'Nvidia gets a breather but Jensen Huang shouldn't'. ICYMI: global semiconductor trade now exceeds oil and gas trade.
items.angle: Low strategist expectations at the start of a year, combined with breadth washouts, are historically a contrarian positive. The risk is the Fed overtightening.
items.tweetA: Strategists expect almost nothing from the S&P in 2027. The last time consensus was this muted going into a year was late 2022, and 2023 was up 24%. Low expectations are the cheapest thing in this market.
items.tweetB: Muted 2027 consensus, $1T+ hyperscaler capex, the biggest IPOs in history. Either Wall Street doesn't believe the AI capex earns a return, or it's sandbagging. Both can't be wrong.
